question: Celiac disease is a chronic autoimmune disease recognised in Italy as a social disease because the relational isolation it creates is such that the perceived social harm is even greater than the physical harm.

The Italian national health service supports measures aimed at promoting the normal integration of celiac disease sufferers into everyday life by facilitating their inclusion in school, sports and work through fair and safe access to catering services. However, this is not the case for the armed forces, admission to which is subject to being in perfect physical health.
With an eye to enabling celiac disease sufferers to enter public competitions for the armed forces and police in the same way all other citizens, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the exclusion of celiac disease sufferers from the armed forces and police also being an issue in other Member States?
Will it consider sponsoring initiatives to combat this discrimination and ensure greater fairness for celiac disease sufferers in accessing the world of the armed forces and police?
answer: Council Directive 2000/78/EC (the ‘Employment Equality Directive’) prohibits discrimination based on inter alia disability in the field of employment and occupation, including as regards conditions for access to employmen t (1). There is no conclusive case law at EU level as regards the qualification of celiac disease as a disability.

The concept of disability in the Employment Equality Directive must be interpreted as including a condition caused by an illness medically diagnosed as curable or incurable where that illness entails a limitation which results in particular from physical, mental or psychological impairments which in interaction with various barriers may hinder the full and effective participation of the person concerned in professional life on an equal basis with other workers, and the limitation is a long-term one (2).

However, Member States may provide that the Employment Equality Directive, in so far as it relates to discrimination on the grounds of disability and age, shall not apply to the armed forces (3). Italy is among the Member States that made use of this provision, introducing an exemption for the armed forces in relation to both disability and age (4).

Other countries which introduced the same exception are Cyprus, Denmark, France, Greece, Ireland, Lithuania, Malta and Slovakia (5). Moreover, in Germany and the Czech Republic, anti-discrimination rules regulating the armed forces do not cover disability and age (6). The fight against discrimination remains a priority for the Commission in all areas where the latter has the competence to take action.
